title: The pseudounipolar DRG neuron
objective: Describe the pseudounipolar shape of a DRG neuron and why it suits organ-to-cord signalling.

steps.title: One stem that splits in two
steps.body:
A [[DRG]] neuron is **[[pseudounipolar]]**: a single process leaves the cell body and immediately forks into two branches —

- a **peripheral** branch running out to the body (skin, colon, pancreas),
- a **central** branch running into the spinal cord [[dorsal horn]].

The cell body sits off to the side in the ganglion, not between the two ends.

visual.alt: A pseudounipolar DRG neuron: the cell body sits off to the side on a short stem that forks into a peripheral branch to an organ and a central branch into the dorsal horn; a signal travels from the organ up past the fork into the cord.
visual.caption: One stem forks to periphery and cord; the cell body sits off to the side.

steps.prompt: Why is the pseudounipolar shape convenient for your experiments?
options: The cell body itself has to be injected with the virus directly
A virus from the ending reaches the cell body for organ access
It means the neuron effectively has no axon of its own
It blocks the neuron from ever projecting into the cord
steps.explanation: Because the peripheral branch connects to the cell body, a retrograde virus injected into the pancreas travels back and labels exactly the neurons innervating it (the C4 logic).

variants.setup: A DRG neuron is pseudounipolar: a peripheral branch and a central branch share one stem from the cell body.
variants.prompt: Why is that shape convenient for your experiments?
options: The cell body itself has to be injected with the virus directly
A virus from the ending reaches the cell body for organ access
It means the neuron effectively has no axon of its own
It blocks the neuron from ever projecting into the cord
variants.reveal: Retrograde uptake at the organ travels to the shared cell body — how you access organ-specific neurons from the organ.

steps.setup: A sensory signal is generated at the peripheral ending in the colon.
steps.prompt: What path does it take to reach the CNS?
options: Peripheral ending → past the cell body → central branch → cord
Straight from the ending into the brain, skipping the cord entirely
Ending → ventral root → out to the muscle it controls
It stays within the organ and never reaches the CNS
steps.reveal: The signal travels along the peripheral branch, past the DRG cell body, down the central branch, and into the spinal cord dorsal horn — where the next lesson picks up the central side.

variants.prompt: What path does a DRG sensory signal take to reach the CNS?
options: Peripheral ending → past the cell body → central branch → cord
Straight from the ending into the brain, skipping the cord entirely
Ending → ventral root → out to the muscle it controls
It stays within the organ and never reaches the CNS
variants.explanation: The signal runs from the peripheral ending, past the off-to-the-side cell body, up the central branch into the dorsal horn.

steps.prompt: Label the parts of this pseudounipolar DRG neuron.
steps.explanation: The cell body sits in the DRG; one branch runs centrally to the dorsal horn, the other peripherally to the target organ.
